audiences/academic.json.name: Academic
audiences/academic.json.summary: Researchers, professors, and students expecting rigorous methodology, citations, and evidence-based conclusions.
audiences/academic.json.description: Researchers, professors, and students who expect rigorous methodology, citations, and evidence-based conclusions. Cite every source, show confidence intervals, be transparent about method, and leave marketing language out. Chart density can be high; 20-50 slides with time reserved for questions.

audiences/all-hands.json.name: All Hands
audiences/all-hands.json.summary: The full company — mixed roles, mixed seniority, looking for context, signal, and inclusion.
audiences/all-hands.json.description: An all-hands audience spans the whole company. Frame the period in terms anyone can grasp: what we did, what mattered, and what's next. Highlight people and teams; surface successes and challenges; close on a forward-looking note. Avoid lapsing into function-specific jargon.

audiences/board.json.name: Board of Directors
audiences/board.json.summary: Directors with fiduciary responsibility who balance oversight, advice, and approval.
audiences/board.json.description: The board is governance-first. They want a complete picture: financial health, key metrics, functional updates, risks, and forward-looking topics. Surface bad news honestly — under-disclosure erodes trust faster than the problems themselves. Bring specific asks that turn the meeting into a working session rather than a recital.

audiences/candidates.json.name: Candidates
audiences/candidates.json.summary: Potential hires evaluating company, role, and people.
audiences/candidates.json.description: Candidates are weighing a major life decision and have many alternatives. Lead with mission and why-now, show the team they'll work with, and be honest about the stage. Avoid generic recruiting copy — specifics build trust faster than polish.

audiences/customer.json.name: Customer
audiences/customer.json.summary: End customers receiving product demos, onboarding presentations, or business reviews.
audiences/customer.json.description: Customers receiving product demos, onboarding, or business reviews. Speak in their language, focus on the value they realize, keep visuals simple, and use strong product screenshots. Keep chart density low; 10-20 slides.

audiences/engineering-team.json.name: Engineering Team
audiences/engineering-team.json.summary: Practitioners building the system; they want depth, mechanism, and tradeoffs.
audiences/engineering-team.json.description: Engineers tune out generalities and tune in to specifics. Show benchmarks with conditions, architecture diagrams with constraints, and tradeoffs you actually considered. Internal jargon is fine — assume the room shares it. Leave room for questions; engineering audiences engage best when they can poke at the proposal.

audiences/executive.json.name: Executive
audiences/executive.json.summary: C-suite and senior leadership focused on strategic decisions, ROI, and big-picture outcomes. Highly time-constrained.
audiences/executive.json.description: C-suite and senior leaders deciding on strategy, ROI, and big-picture outcomes with very little time. Lead with the conclusion and keep to one insight per slide; set the key numbers in bold type and use as few bullet points as possible. Keep chart density low and the deck to 10-15 slides at most.

audiences/general-public.json.name: General Public
audiences/general-public.json.summary: Mixed non-expert audience with no assumed domain knowledge.
audiences/general-public.json.description: A mixed audience of non-experts with no assumed domain knowledge. Prefer analogies to data, use only simple charts, set large text for accessibility, and structure the talk as a story. Keep chart density low; 10-15 slides.

audiences/media.json.name: Media & Press
audiences/media.json.summary: Journalists, analysts, and media professionals seeking newsworthy insights and quotable statistics.
audiences/media.json.description: Journalists, analysts, and media professionals looking for newsworthy insight and quotable statistics. Make headline numbers prominent, attribute every figure clearly, design for print, and add embargo notes when needed. Moderate chart density; 8-12 slides in press-kit format.

audiences/partner.json.name: Partner / Channel
audiences/partner.json.summary: Strategic partners, resellers, or channel organizations needing positioning and enablement content.
audiences/partner.json.description: Strategic partners, resellers, and channel organizations who need positioning and enablement content. Highlight partner economics, include co-branding guidelines, state the value proposition for their customers, and link enablement resources. Moderate chart density; 15-25 slides.

audiences/regulatory.json.name: Regulatory / Compliance
audiences/regulatory.json.summary: Government agencies, auditors, or compliance bodies reviewing adherence to rules and standards.
audiences/regulatory.json.description: Government agencies, auditors, and compliance bodies reviewing adherence to rules and standards. Lead with evidence, date-stamp material, cite document references, and map each claim to the requirement it satisfies. Moderate chart density; 20-40 slides with an appendix.

audiences/sales.json.name: Sales
audiences/sales.json.summary: Sales team or prospective customers focused on product benefits, competitive differentiation, and ROI justification.
audiences/sales.json.description: Sales teams and prospective customers weighing product benefits, competitive differentiation, and ROI. Put customer success stories first, back claims with visual proof points, state the value proposition plainly, and close on a strong call to action. Moderate chart density; 15-25 slides.

audiences/technical.json.summary: Engineers, data scientists, and technical specialists requiring precision, methodology details, and system-level understanding.
audiences/technical.json.description: Engineers, data scientists, and technical specialists who expect precision, methodology, and system-level understanding. Show the methodology and cite data sources, prefer technical diagrams to metaphors, and do not shy away from dense information. Chart density can be high; 20-40 slides is normal.

narratives/board-meeting.json.name: Board Meeting
narratives/board-meeting.json.summary: Comprehensive board update covering CEO commentary, key metrics, financials, functional updates, and forward-looking topics. Designed to keep directors informed, aligned, and ready to advise. Use the full set for in-person quarterly meetings; trim sections for monthly checkpoints.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Set the tone for the meeting and walk through the agenda in one slide. Signal which sections are for discussion versus information so directors know where their time is most valuable.

beats.name: CEO Update
beats.description: Deliver the CEO's view of the period: what changed, what mattered, where the company stands. Two or three sentences in the speaker's voice — board members read this slide first.

beats.name: Highlights
beats.description: Share major successes across the business. Customer wins, launches, hires, milestones. Specific and brief; this is the slide that sets the tone, not the slide that proves the case.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Address the obstacles facing the business honestly. Boards earn their value when surfaced to real problems; under-disclosure here erodes trust faster than the problems themselves.

beats.name: Company Needs
beats.description: Identify where the business needs the board's help: introductions, decisions, advice. Specific asks turn the meeting from a report into a working session.

beats.name: Funnel Metrics
beats.description: Discuss the sales pipeline: leads, conversion, velocity, win rate. Use the metrics that match the company's current motion; resist the temptation to show the same chart you showed last quarter for continuity's sake.

beats.name: Engagement Metrics
beats.description: Analyze customer interaction: usage, retention, NPS, expansion. Show whether the product is being loved or only being bought.

beats.name: Financial Metrics
beats.description: Review fiscal health: revenue, gross margin, burn, runway, cash. One slide directors can scan in twenty seconds and trust the numbers on.

beats.name: Performance vs Plan
beats.description: Compare actuals to plan across the metrics that matter most. Variance is the slide directors will probe; show your work, name the drivers, propose adjustments.

beats.name: Org Chart
beats.description: Present the team structure and any key changes since the last meeting. Directors track org evolution as a leading indicator; help them see hires, departures, and reshapes clearly.

beats.name: Product Roadmap
beats.description: Highlight the product plan and what ships when. Pair each major bet with the customer or business outcome it serves.

beats.name: Quality
beats.description: Showcase the product quality bar: reliability, defect rates, support outcomes. Directors take quality as a proxy for engineering culture; let the data speak.

beats.name: Engineering Update
beats.description: Communicate technical progress, key bets, and platform investments. Translate engineering work into business consequences directors can evaluate.

beats.name: Marketing Update
beats.description: Update on demand-gen, brand, and category-shaping efforts. Connect spend to pipeline and pipeline to revenue; avoid 'campaigns we ran' lists.

beats.name: Business Development Update
beats.description: Speak to growth initiatives: partnerships, channels, alliances. Each entry should have a stage, an owner, and a credible upside.

beats.name: Operations Update
beats.description: Discuss day-to-day operations: people ops, finance, legal, IT. Brief but explicit — directors notice when ops is missing.

beats.name: Special Topic 1
beats.description: Discuss the period's first deep-dive topic. This is where the board does its highest-leverage work; pose the question, show the analysis, ask for their view.

beats.name: Special Topic 2
beats.description: Cover the second deep-dive topic, framed the same way. Two specials per meeting; more, and the meeting becomes a recital.

beats.name: Feedback
beats.description: Elicit the board's perspective with concrete prompts. The strength of board governance is in its candor — invite it explicitly.

beats.name: Formalities
beats.description: Conclude with the necessary governance items: votes, approvals, committee reports, document acknowledgments. Run them efficiently and document the outcomes.

beats.name: Closing Remarks
beats.description: Close with concluding observations and the agenda for the next meeting. End on a forward-looking note; directors should leave knowing what to watch.

narratives/business-narrative.json.name: Business Narrative
narratives/business-narrative.json.summary: Tell a business strategy or solution as a story: setting, challenge, tension, hero, plan, outcome. Useful for internal alignment decks, town halls, and any audience that responds better to story shape than to bullet lists.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Engage the audience and set expectations for the next twenty minutes. Tell them you're going to tell them a story — and then start telling it. Avoid a separate agenda slide; the introduction is the first scene.

beats.name: Setting
beats.description: Establish the world the story takes place in: the team, the market, the moment. Just enough context that the challenge will feel meaningful when it arrives.

beats.name: Challenge
beats.description: Identify the issue at hand. Concrete, specific, attributable. The challenge is the inciting incident — the thing that pulled the rest of the story into motion.

beats.name: Tension
beats.description: Raise the stakes. What happens if the challenge isn't met? Quantify the cost, name the people affected, surface the trade-offs that make the choice hard. Tension is what makes the audience lean in.

beats.name: Solution
beats.description: Reveal the strategy or hero of the story. Lead with what changes for the audience or customer when the solution is in place. This is the turn from problem to promise.

beats.name: Implementation
beats.description: Describe the path to success. Phases, owners, milestones, key bets. Show the audience that the solution has weight behind it — not just intent.

beats.name: Recap
beats.description: Bring the audience back to the surface with a clear summary of what was said and decided. Echo the language from the opening so the story feels closed.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Reinforce the key message and the call to action. End on the line you most want repeated in tomorrow's hallway conversations.
beats.instructions: Reinforce takeaways and call to action

narratives/business-review.json.name: Business Review
narratives/business-review.json.summary: Full-loop review of recent activities to identify achievements, address challenges, and plan improvements. Goes deeper than a status update — closer to a customer-facing or partner-facing relationship review.

beats.name: Logo
beats.description: Cover slide with logos and the review period. Establishes brand identity and signals the level of formality the rest of the deck will hold to.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Frame the meeting context and the goals for the next hour. What you'll cover, what decisions you want, what you don't intend to relitigate.

beats.name: Review
beats.description: Outline the recent activities in scope: launches, projects, programs. Just enough scope-setting that the rest of the deck has shared vocabulary.

beats.name: Successes
beats.description: Recognize the achievements in the review window. Lead with outcomes the audience cares about, not effort. Specific moves earn more credibility than aggregate progress.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Address the problems faced honestly. What didn't work, what's still hard. Naming challenges in front of the audience earns more trust than letting them ask.

beats.name: Solutions
beats.description: Discuss the fixes already implemented. Pair each with the result it produced, or, if it's still in flight, with the leading indicator you're watching.

beats.name: Outcome
beats.description: Display the results achieved across the review window. Let the data carry the slide; supporting commentary should explain context, not inflate the numbers.

beats.name: Insights
beats.description: Highlight the key learnings. What was confirmed, what surprised you, what the audience should take away. Insights are the slides people quote in follow-on meetings.

beats.name: Future Strategy
beats.description: Define the next steps and the strategic direction that follows from the review. Specific enough to sequence; flexible enough to adapt.

beats.name: Feedback
beats.description: Capture audience thoughts. Two or three explicit prompts where you want input or alignment. The strength of a relationship review is in the conversation it provokes.

beats.name: Next Review
beats.description: Plan for follow-up: when the next review happens, what evidence you'll bring, what decisions are deferred until then. Continuity is the point of the cadence.

beats.name: Closing
beats.description: Recap and express optimism about the path forward. Close with the next concrete step and the people responsible for it.

narratives/capacity-planning.json.name: Capacity Planning
narratives/capacity-planning.json.summary: Workforce and operational capacity-planning arc: kickoff, urgency, current state, projection, tactics, implementation, revision, conclusion. For decks where leadership must decide whether the organization has enough resources to meet upcoming demand.

beats.name: Kickoff
beats.description: Introduce what the planning exercise covers and the decision you need from the audience. Frame the time horizon and the resources in scope so the rest of the deck stays bounded.

beats.name: Urgency
beats.description: Show why this is the right moment to plan capacity. Pipeline shifts, hiring freezes, operational stress signals. Urgency turns capacity from an annual ritual into a decision the audience leans into.

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Highlight the current resource picture: people, tools, infrastructure, vendor capacity. Show utilization, not just headcount. The audience should know where slack and stress live today.

beats.name: Projection
beats.description: Predict future demand under your base case and a sensitivity case. Tie demand to specific drivers — pipeline, launches, seasonality — so the audience can challenge the assumptions, not just the totals.

beats.name: Tactics
beats.description: Suggest the strategies for closing any gap: hiring, automation, outsourcing, prioritization. Each tactic should map to a specific demand driver and a defensible cost.

beats.name: Implementation
beats.description: Discuss how the plan gets deployed. Sequencing, owners, dependencies, lead times. Capacity decisions slip the most when the rollout isn't planned with the same rigor as the sizing.

beats.name: Revision
beats.description: Define the leading indicators that would trigger a re-plan, and the cadence of review. Capacity plans age fast; show the audience how the plan stays alive.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Wrap up with the specific recommendations and the decisions you need today. End with the next checkpoint and what evidence will be on the table at it.

narratives/challenge-resolution.json.name: Challenge → Resolution
narratives/challenge-resolution.json.summary: Identify a current business challenge, trace its origins, and recommend an actionable resolution. Useful for management consulting, internal strategy memos, and any deck where the audience needs a clear path from problem to plan.

beats.name: Hook
beats.description: Open with a specific, visible signal of the challenge — a metric heading the wrong way, a customer story, a competitive event. The hook should make the audience nod that yes, this matters.

beats.name: Dilemma
beats.description: State the challenge plainly. What is failing, who is feeling it, and why has it now risen to a level that demands a decision? The dilemma must feel real, not academic.

beats.name: Backdrop
beats.description: Provide the context behind the dilemma: how it formed, what's been tried, what constraints exist. Just enough history that the audience trusts your diagnosis without drowning in detail.

beats.name: Remedy
beats.description: Propose the resolution. Lead with the recommendation, then sketch the approach. Be opinionated — vague remedies invite vague responses.

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Demonstrate why the remedy will work. Comparable cases, supporting data, or pilot results. Choose evidence that addresses the audience's most likely objection, not the one easiest to answer.

beats.name: Motivate
beats.description: Make the case for acting now. Quantify the cost of delay and the upside of decisive action. Help the audience picture the room a quarter from now if they say yes.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Recap the challenge, the remedy, and the specific decision you need from the audience. End with a clear ask, not a summary slide.

narratives/change-story.json.name: Change Story
narratives/change-story.json.summary: A change management narrative that addresses the emotional and rational objections employees face when asked to change.
narratives/change-story.json.description: A change management narrative that addresses the emotional and rational objections people face when asked to change. Establish the burning platform, explain why the timing is urgent, show the chosen path and the alternatives it was chosen over, make the stakes concrete for the organization, the team, and individuals, and close on a shared vision in which the audience is the protagonist. The tone is motivational and empathetic: it acknowledges that change is hard while building conviction. Best for organizational change, transformation announcements, restructuring communications, and all-hands meetings; typical decks run 8-15 slides.

beats.name: Why Change
beats.description: Acknowledge the current state and the external or internal forces requiring change. Don't skip the burning platform.
beats.instructions: Explain why the current state cannot continue.

beats.name: Why Now
beats.description: Explain the urgency. What changes if we wait? What window is closing?
beats.instructions: Make the timing urgent and concrete.

beats.name: Why This Way
beats.description: Show that alternatives were considered. Build trust by demonstrating thoughtful decision-making.
beats.instructions: Describe the proposed path and why it fits.

beats.name: What's at Stake
beats.description: Make consequences concrete for the organization, the team, and individuals. Avoid abstract language.
beats.instructions: Show the risks and rewards attached to the choice.

beats.name: How We Win Together
beats.description: Paint a shared vision of success. Make the audience the protagonist of the new story.
beats.instructions: Close with shared ownership and first commitments.

narratives/classic-story.json.name: Classic Story
narratives/classic-story.json.summary: Movie-style narrative arc applied to any topic: open the scene, introduce the villain, raise the stakes, send in the hero, deliver the plan, and close with hope. A versatile go-to when you need to make information feel like a story.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Capture attention with a vivid moment, image, or question that sets the world of the story. The audience should immediately know what kind of room they're in. Avoid agendas — the opening is the first scene, not a preamble.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Establish what's normal in this world before anything goes wrong. Just enough background for the audience to feel the stakes when the villain shows up. Keep it tight; backstory is fuel, not the engine.

beats.name: Villain
beats.description: Introduce the antagonist — a problem, a competitor, a market force, an inertia. Give it a face and a name where you can. The clearer the villain, the more the audience cares about how the story turns out.

beats.name: Despair
beats.description: Show what's at risk if the villain wins. Emphasize the human or business cost of inaction. Don't rush past this beat — the discomfort here is what makes the resolution land.

beats.name: Hero
beats.description: Reveal the hero of the story. Often this is the audience themselves, your team, or your product. Frame the hero by what they uniquely bring to the fight, not by their résumé.

beats.name: Plan
beats.description: Walk through how the hero defeats the villain. Concrete, sequential, credible. Generic plans signal weak heroes; specific plans earn belief that the ending you're promising is reachable.

beats.name: Closing
beats.description: End with the resolution and the lesson. Show what the world looks like after the villain loses, and leave the audience with the feeling — and the line — they'll repeat afterwards.

narratives/company-intro.json.name: Company Intro
narratives/company-intro.json.summary: Standard company-overview deck: who you are, what's distinctive about you, who you serve, and why they win. Built for first-touch sales meetings, partner intros, and 'about us' decks attached to outbound emails.

beats.name: Logo
beats.description: Cover slide with the logo, tagline, and a single line of positioning. Set the visual tone — confident, branded, uncluttered.

beats.name: About
beats.description: Capture the company in three or four lines: what you do, who you do it for, and how long you've been at it. Avoid jargon; an outsider should grok the business in fifteen seconds.

beats.name: Competitive Advantage
beats.description: State the one or two things you do that the alternatives can't. Frame it as a structural advantage, not a feature list. The audience should leave able to repeat the differentiator in their own words.

beats.name: Company Story
beats.description: Share the founding insight or origin moment — why this company exists, told as a short story. Specific people, specific problems, a specific 'aha.' Story beats biography.

beats.name: Offerings
beats.description: Map the products and services into a coherent picture. Show how they fit together rather than listing them flat. The shape of the portfolio is itself a message.

beats.name: Ideal Customer
beats.description: Define who you serve best. Industry, size, role, situation. Specificity here helps the audience self-select and signals you understand the customer well enough to be choosy.

beats.name: Key Benefits
beats.description: Translate offerings into three to five customer outcomes. Lead with the result, not the mechanism. Each benefit should answer 'what becomes easier or better for me?'

beats.name: Success Story
beats.description: Tell one named customer's story with concrete before/after metrics. A single specific story is more persuasive than a logo grid; pick one that mirrors the audience you're presenting to.

beats.name: Closing & CTA
beats.description: Close with one line of why now and one specific next step — a discovery call, a pilot, a partner program. End with contact info that's easy to act on without searching.

narratives/conference-talk.json.name: Conference Talk
narratives/conference-talk.json.summary: Stage-talk arc for a 15–45 minute conference or industry-event session: hook the room, promise a payoff, deliver evidence, expose the underlying mechanism, show how to apply it, and end with a memorable recap. Engineered for audiences that came to learn something they can use Monday.

beats.name: Hook
beats.description: Earn the first sixty seconds with a story, surprising claim, or vivid moment. Make the audience curious enough to put their phones down. Avoid agendas, bios, and 'today I'm going to talk about' openings — those are filler that competes with your real opening.

beats.name: Promise
beats.description: Tell the audience exactly what they'll know, feel, or be able to do by the end of the talk. A clear promise sets the implicit contract for the next thirty minutes and lets you redirect attention later when needed.

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Deliver the substantive case for your promise. Data, examples, demonstrations, or strong stories — whatever a skeptical attendee would need to update their beliefs. This is the densest section of the talk; pace and visualize accordingly.

beats.name: Mechanism
beats.description: Reveal the underlying principle or framework that explains why the evidence holds. The mechanism is what audiences quote later — the moment of 'oh, that's why.' Keep it crisp and namable.

beats.name: Application
beats.description: Show the audience how to use the mechanism in their own work. Concrete, specific, low-friction first steps. The talk earns its keep here — abstract insight without an applied path is forgotten by lunch.

beats.name: Recap
beats.description: Restate the promise, the mechanism, and the call to action in a single short slide. Give the audience the line they'll repeat to a colleague and the one image that will stick with them after the lights come up.

narratives/data-story.json.name: Data Story
narratives/data-story.json.summary: A data-first narrative that builds from evidence to insight to action, ideal for analysts and data-driven teams.
narratives/data-story.json.description: A data-first narrative that builds from evidence to insight to action. Set the analytical context and the question the data answers, reveal the headline finding, walk through the supporting analysis and its sources, explain what it means for the business, then make a specific recommendation with its confidence level and assumptions. The tone is analytical and inductive: it builds up from data to insight. Best for analytical briefings, data team presentations, research readouts, and business reviews; typical decks run 6-15 slides.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Frame why this analysis matters now. What question is this data answering?
beats.instructions: Set up the business question and data scope.

beats.name: Key Finding
beats.description: State the single most important thing the data shows. One slide, one insight.
beats.instructions: State the one finding the audience must remember.

beats.name: Analysis
beats.description: Unpack the data rigorously. Show sources, methodology, and supporting charts.
beats.instructions: Explain the drivers behind the finding.

beats.name: Implications
beats.description: Translate findings into business language. What does this mean for strategy, operations, or customers?
beats.instructions: Translate the analysis into business consequences.

beats.name: Recommendation
beats.description: Make an explicit, actionable recommendation backed by the data. Include confidence level and assumptions.
beats.instructions: Recommend the next decision or action.

narratives/early-startup-pitch.json.name: Early-Stage Startup Pitch
narratives/early-startup-pitch.json.summary: Seed and pre-seed pitch arc tuned for vision-heavy stories where revenue and traction are still thin. Anchors the narrative in market change, founder insight, and credible early signal — not metrics yet.

beats.name: Logo
beats.description: Cover slide with the company name, logo, and one-line positioning. Simple, branded, confident.

beats.name: Monumental Change
beats.description: Open by naming a large, undeniable shift in the world. Tech, regulatory, behavioral. The shift is the reason this company exists — investors should feel its weight before they hear about the product.

beats.name: Past Struggle
beats.description: Show what the world tried to do about the problem before the shift, and why those approaches fell short. Honest credit to predecessors makes the new game more credible.

beats.name: Innovative Breakthrough
beats.description: Present the founding insight or breakthrough that makes a new approach possible. This is the 'secret' the company is built on — name it plainly.

beats.name: Unique Offering
beats.description: Detail the product or service. Lead with the customer-visible thing they touch; the architecture can wait. Show why this offering is structurally different from the past struggle.

beats.name: Costly Issues
beats.description: Quantify the pain customers experience without your offering. Time, dollars, opportunity cost. Specific numbers convert sympathy into urgency.

beats.name: Effective Solutions
beats.description: Demonstrate the customer outcome your offering produces. Before/after numbers from early users, even small N. Early-stage pitches are won by leading indicators, not by trailing ones.

beats.name: Unit Economics
beats.description: Explain the financial model. Cost to acquire, gross margin, payback. Investors don't expect maturity — they expect that you've thought about it.

beats.name: Talented Team
beats.description: Introduce the founders and key early hires. Show why this team uniquely sees and can execute on this opportunity. Insight beats résumé at the seed stage.

beats.name: Traction
beats.description: Showcase the early signal: pilots, design partners, waitlist, retention data, anything credible. Frame it honestly — investors at this stage discount inflation aggressively.

beats.name: Investment Opportunity
beats.description: Detail the round size, structure, and use of funds. Tie the raise to specific milestones it takes the company to. Specificity here signals operational maturity.

beats.name: Closing Logo
beats.description: Close on the brand and contact info. Leave the room with the line you most want repeated when the partner pitches you to the rest of the firm.

narratives/educate.json.name: Educate
narratives/educate.json.summary: Engaging-explainer arc inspired by Mary Roach: surprise the audience with a fact, walk them through evidence and anecdote, scrutinize the assumptions, then close on a memorable insight. For technical, scientific, or analytical talks that need to feel more like discovery than instruction.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Introduce the topic in a way that respects the audience's time and curiosity. Frame why this question is worth asking, and signal the shape of the journey ahead without giving away the destination.

beats.name: Surprising Fact
beats.description: Lead with a single curious fact that recasts how the audience thinks about the topic. The fact should be small, specific, and unforgettable — the cognitive door the rest of the talk walks through.

beats.name: Experiment
beats.description: Walk through a method, study, or thought experiment that probes the surprising fact. Show how knowledge here gets made — the audience should feel like they're shoulder-to-shoulder with the investigator.

beats.name: Amusing Anecdote
beats.description: Drop in a story or moment from the field that brings the topic to human scale. Personality and humor here keep the audience leaning forward; technical depth without warmth loses the room.

beats.name: Intriguing Information
beats.description: Layer in the more complex data or detail. By this point the audience is invested enough to do real work alongside you. Visualize generously — make the numbers tangible.

beats.name: Skeptical Scrutiny
beats.description: Question the easy interpretations. Challenge the audience's defaults and your own. Showing where the evidence is contested is what separates a teacher from a publicist.

beats.name: Extraordinary Explanation
beats.description: Present the most counterintuitive or beautiful explanation the topic offers. Take your time here — this is the payoff slide the audience came for.

beats.name: Unconventional Use
beats.description: Show an unexpected application or implication of the idea. Surprise reinforces the lesson and gives the audience a story to retell tomorrow.

beats.name: Captivating Conclusion
beats.description: Close with a thoughtful, slightly poetic wrap-up. Echo the surprising fact, name the lesson, and leave the audience with a new question instead of a tidy answer.

narratives/employee-review.json.name: Employee Review
narratives/employee-review.json.summary: Constructive performance-review arc that recognizes work, gives candid feedback, and sets growth goals together. For one-on-one performance conversations and formal year-end reviews.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open with the period covered and the spirit of the conversation: collaborative, honest, growth-focused. Frame the meeting so both sides know what to expect.

beats.name: Performance
beats.description: Review job execution against the role's expectations. Specific examples, dated. Avoid characterizing the person; describe the work and its impact.

beats.name: Achievements
beats.description: Acknowledge what went well. Name the projects, the moves, the moments where the employee made a difference. Specific recognition lands harder than generic praise.

beats.name: Feedback
beats.description: Provide constructive feedback grounded in observation. Distinguish patterns from one-offs. Tell the employee something they can act on, not something they can only feel.

beats.name: Constructive Criticism
beats.description: Suggest improvements in language that respects the employee's intelligence. Pair each piece of criticism with a concrete example and a specific behavior change you'd like to see.

beats.name: Development Opportunities
beats.description: Highlight growth areas and the experiences that could stretch the employee. Frame development as an investment, not a fix.

beats.name: Goals
beats.description: Outline next-period goals together. Specific, measurable, with explicit support. The strongest goals are co-authored, not handed down.

beats.name: Mentoring
beats.description: Encourage continued learning through mentorship, training, peer pairings. Close the review with the message that growth is a shared responsibility, not a one-way evaluation.

narratives/failure-analysis.json.name: Failure Analysis
narratives/failure-analysis.json.summary: Walk through what went wrong, why, and what changes — a structured post-mortem for stakeholder reviews. Pairs honest accountability with a credible recovery plan.

beats.name: Opening Remark
beats.description: Set an empathetic, accountable tone before any analysis. Acknowledge the impact on the people in the room and the customers affected. Authenticity here earns you the credibility you'll need for the rest of the deck.

beats.name: Incident Breakdown
beats.description: Walk through what happened, in time order. Stick to facts: what systems, what users, what timeline. No causal claims yet — just an accurate, neutral reconstruction the audience can trust.

beats.name: Impact Analysis
beats.description: Quantify the damage. Customer-hours lost, revenue at risk, SLA breaches, downstream knock-ons. Be specific and direct; vague impact statements undermine the rest of the post-mortem.

beats.name: Root Cause
beats.description: Trace the failure to its underlying cause, not the most visible symptom. Use a 'five whys' or fishbone framing if useful. Distinguish between the proximate trigger and the systemic conditions that allowed it.

beats.name: Proposed Solutions
beats.description: Present the corrective actions you're taking. Lead with the highest-leverage fix; sequence the rest. For each action, name an owner and a date — solutions without owners are aspirations.

beats.name: Action Plan
beats.description: Lay out the rollout: what ships when, how it's verified, who signs off. Show that 'fixed' has a definition and a deadline, not just intent.

beats.name: Evaluate Outcome
beats.description: Define the metrics that will tell you the fix worked. Pre/post comparisons, monitoring SLOs, error budgets — whatever proves the failure mode is closed and not just deferred.

beats.name: Lessons Learned
beats.description: Distill the broader lessons that outlive this specific incident. What does the team or organization now know that it didn't before? What patterns will you watch for elsewhere?

beats.name: Preventive Measures
beats.description: List the systemic safeguards being added — process changes, automated checks, on-call procedures, review gates. Show how this category of failure becomes harder to recur, not just this specific instance.

beats.name: Closing Thoughts
beats.description: Close with humility and forward momentum. Re-affirm accountability, thank the audience for their patience, and signal confidence in the path forward without overclaiming.

narratives/focus.json.name: Focus
narratives/focus.json.summary: Long-term, principle-driven business arc inspired by Jeff Bezos's 1997 letter to shareholders: name the focus, account for performance, articulate the framework, and commit to the discipline that will keep the company on track. For founder letters, all-hands narratives, and any deck where the audience needs to feel the through-line.

beats.name: Welcome
beats.description: Open with a brief framing of what this update is for and what you intend to leave the audience with. Set the tone — long-term, candid, principle-driven.

beats.name: Accomplishments
beats.description: Showcase the period's most material wins, briefly. The audience came for what's next; wins earn permission for the harder slides ahead, but they aren't the headline.

beats.name: Potential
beats.description: Detail the market and customer opportunities ahead. Size them honestly and connect them to the work already underway. Potential without specifics reads as wishful.

beats.name: Competitive Edge
beats.description: Reveal the strategic positioning that gives the business its advantage. Frame it as a structural moat, not a list of features. The audience should be able to repeat the moat in their own words.

beats.name: Long-Term Vision
beats.description: Emphasize the long-term view that anchors decisions. Quarters serve years; years serve decades. Anchor the audience in the time horizon you actually run the business on.

beats.name: Performance Metrics
beats.description: Illuminate the indicators that show the long-term thesis is working. Choose metrics that compound — retention, NPS, unit economics — over those that flatter.

beats.name: Growth Achievement
beats.description: Certify the tangible progress against the long-term plan. Year-over-year, cohort behavior, expanded reach. Growth, in this beat, is evidence that the strategy is real.

beats.name: Strategic Framework
beats.description: Explain the principles that guide decisions. Customer obsession, long-term thinking, frugality, ownership — whatever the actual operating discipline is. Principles are the connective tissue between strategy and behavior.

beats.name: Expansion
beats.description: Detail the next areas of growth: products, segments, geographies. Tie each to the principles above so the audience sees expansion as continuity rather than scatter.

beats.name: Future Objectives
beats.description: Forecast the targets and commitments for the period ahead. Be specific enough to be held accountable. Vague objectives are how strategies erode.

beats.name: Acknowledgment
beats.description: Recognize the contributions of teams, customers, and partners that made the period possible. Specific names land harder than blanket thanks.

beats.name: Closing Remarks
beats.description: Recap the focus, thank the audience, and inspire the work ahead. End with the line you most want quoted in tomorrow's newsletter.

narratives/golden-circle.json.name: Golden Circle (Why / How / What)
narratives/golden-circle.json.summary: Simon Sinek's keynote arc: lead with belief, follow with method, finish with proof. Best for brand stories, mission-driven keynotes, and any deck where the audience needs to feel why before they can evaluate what.

beats.name: Why
beats.description: Open with the belief or purpose that animates the work. Why does this exist, and why should anyone care beyond commerce? State it plainly and emotionally — the why is meant to be felt before it is understood.

beats.name: How
beats.description: Translate the belief into the principles that guide how you operate. The values, decisions, and trade-offs that make your approach distinctive. The 'how' is what people who share your why recognize as familiar.

beats.name: What
beats.description: Show the products, services, or outputs that the why and how produce. Concrete examples, not abstractions. The what is the artifact of the belief — proof that the why is more than rhetoric.

beats.name: Proof
beats.description: Demonstrate the impact in lives, customers, or outcomes. Stories beat statistics here; specific people and moments earn the audience's belief better than aggregate numbers. End with proof that what you do works because of why you do it.

beats.name: Invitation
beats.description: Close by inviting the audience to share the belief — to buy, build, join, or evangelize. The strongest invitations don't argue; they assume alignment and offer a way in.

narratives/heros-journey.json.name: Hero's Journey
narratives/heros-journey.json.summary: Storytelling framework that takes the audience on an emotional journey of change and growth.
narratives/heros-journey.json.description: A storytelling framework that takes the audience on an emotional journey of change and growth. Show where things started, the obstacle that forced a change, the path taken and the obstacles overcome, the turning point, and the improved reality with the lessons it taught. The tone is narrative: it builds an emotional arc and invites the audience to identify with the protagonist, whether that is a customer, a team, or the company itself. Best for case studies, brand stories, and change management; typical decks run 5-10 slides (brand story, startup pitch, culture deck, change story).

beats.name: Status Quo
beats.description: Establish the starting point. What was normal life like before the challenge?
beats.instructions: Establish the starting world before change.

beats.name: Challenge
beats.description: Introduce the disruption or opportunity that demanded change.
beats.instructions: Introduce the disruption that makes change necessary.

beats.name: Journey
beats.description: Walk through the process of transformation. Include obstacles overcome.
beats.instructions: Walk through the path, obstacles, and choices.

beats.name: Transformation
beats.description: Show the pivotal moment or insight that changed everything.
beats.instructions: Show the turning point that changes the outcome.

beats.name: New Reality
beats.description: Reveal the improved state and the lessons that will benefit your audience.
beats.instructions: Reveal the improved state and lesson learned.
