records.summary: Tight rhythm-of-business arc for weekly progress reports — designed for fifteen-to-thirty-minute team check-ins.

records.name: Status Update
records.summary: Concise progress-report arc for keeping a stakeholder informed: headline, brief, progress, results, plan, feedback.

records.name: Performance Review
records.summary: Analytical review of individual, team, or company performance grounded in metrics and adjustments for the next period.

records.name: Survey Analysis
records.summary: Structured walk-through of survey results: topic, executive summary, methodology, findings, analysis, implications, recommendations.

records.name: Trend Analysis
records.summary: Identify and discuss data-driven patterns to understand performance and forecast what's next.

records.name: Data Story
records.summary: A data-first narrative that builds from evidence to insight to action, ideal for analysts and data-driven teams.

records.name: Employee Review
records.summary: Constructive performance-review arc that recognizes work, gives candid feedback, and sets growth goals together.

records.name: Performance Improvement Plan
records.summary: Structured PIP arc that helps a struggling employee see expectations, understand the gap, and walk a credible improvement path.

records.name: Capacity Planning
records.summary: Workforce and operational capacity-planning arc: kickoff, urgency, current state, projection, tactics, implementation, revision.

narratives/innovation.json.name: Innovation
narratives/innovation.json.summary: Keynote-style product reveal inspired by Steve Jobs's 2007 iPhone launch: stage-set, reveal, demonstrate, wow, differentiate, reframe the category, build excitement, call to action, and thank the audience. For category-defining product moments.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Set the stage. Tell the audience they're about to see something that matters, without yet showing it. The pause before the reveal is part of the reveal.

beats.name: Revelation
beats.description: Announce the product. One image, one name, one sentence. Anything more competes with the moment. The slide should feel like the curtain going up.

beats.name: Demonstration
beats.description: Show the product in real use. Choose a single defining workflow that captures what the product does and how it feels. Live beats canned wherever possible.

beats.name: Wow Factor
beats.description: Highlight the cutting-edge feature that earns the headline. One thing, presented well — the audience should leave able to repeat it in a sentence.

beats.name: Differentiation
beats.description: Make the contrast with existing alternatives unmistakable. Use comparisons that the audience already understands; don't argue against straw versions of the competition.

beats.name: Revolution
beats.description: Reframe the category. Show how the product changes what the playing field looks like, not just where you sit on it. This is the slide pundits will quote.

beats.name: Excitement
beats.description: Build anticipation around what's next: availability, partnerships, what the audience can imagine doing with the product. Excitement is how the room exits the keynote into the world.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Give the audience the action that channels the excitement. Pre-order, try it, tell others. Be specific so the energy converts into behavior.

beats.name: Gratitude
beats.description: Thank the team that built it and the audience that came. Brief, sincere, not perfunctory. The closing thanks is the period at the end of the keynote.

narratives/justice.json.name: Justice
narratives/justice.json.summary: Advocacy arc inspired by the rhetorical structure of Martin Luther King Jr.'s 'I Have a Dream' speech: name the inequality, share the dream, build urgency, layer further visions, emphasize unity, call to action, and close on hope. For movement-building keynotes and mission-driven speeches.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Set the stage with a moment that earns the audience's full attention. Speak in the moral register the rest of the talk will require. Avoid throat-clearing — open as if the speech were already underway.

beats.name: Give Context
beats.description: Place the issue in its historical and current context. What promises were made, what has and hasn't been kept. Context turns the speech from opinion into accountability.
beats.instructions: Put in historical and current context

beats.name: Highlight Inequality
beats.description: Show specific, undeniable examples of the inequality at issue. Concrete moments and people, not abstractions. The audience should feel the gap between what is and what was promised.

beats.name: Share the Dream
beats.description: Describe the future you envision in vivid, specific detail. The dream must be both ambitious and recognizable — a world the audience can picture themselves living in.

beats.name: Create Urgency
beats.description: Explain why the time for change is now. The cost of waiting, the moment that won't return. Urgency converts shared vision into shared movement.
beats.instructions: Explain the need for immediate change

beats.name: Continue the Vision
beats.description: Layer additional visions of the future in parallel structure. Repetition and rhythm build momentum the way a single image cannot.
beats.instructions: Continue to elaborate on your vision

beats.name: Emphasize Unity
beats.description: Speak to the collective power of the audience together. Name common ground that crosses lines the issue normally divides. Unity is the engine that turns dream into march.

beats.name: Final Vision
beats.description: Deliver one more, fully realized vision of the world you're calling for. Specific enough to be remembered, expansive enough to inspire.
beats.instructions: Further share dreams of ideal in-depth

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Ask the audience to participate in the change. Be specific about what 'doing something' looks like — show, march, give, vote, organize. Vague CTAs produce vague action.
beats.instructions: Ask audience to participate in change

beats.name: Show Determination
beats.description: Encourage persistence in the face of resistance. Acknowledge what will be hard. Determination, named honestly, is more durable than easy optimism.

beats.name: Create Hope
beats.description: Close on hope grounded in evidence: progress already made, victories already won, ground already moved. Hope as a conclusion lands strongest when it sounds like it has been earned.

narratives/marketing-strategy.json.name: Marketing Strategy
narratives/marketing-strategy.json.summary: Comprehensive go-to-market strategy arc structured around the 4Ps. Use for category launches, annual marketing plans, and any deck where the audience needs to see customer, market, competition, and tactics in one coherent picture.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open by establishing the product or service this strategy is for, and what window of time it covers. One slide that tells the audience exactly which world they're being asked to weigh in on.

beats.name: Objective
beats.description: State the marketing goals in measurable terms: revenue, pipeline, awareness, share. Two or three goals, ranked. Goals without ranking get equal energy and equal mediocrity.

beats.name: Customer
beats.description: Detail the target audience. Segments, jobs-to-be-done, decision criteria, where they live in the buying cycle. Specificity here is the foundation everything else stands on.

beats.name: Market
beats.description: Describe the market landscape: size, growth, segments, behavioral trends. Use external data for credibility and your own research for nuance. Show how the market is changing, not just how big it is.

beats.name: Competition
beats.description: Map the competitive set honestly. Direct, indirect, and substitutes. A 2x2 or feature-comparison framework helps; what matters is that the audience trusts your read of the field.

beats.name: Strategy
beats.description: Articulate the marketing approach in one sentence and a single supporting frame. Positioning, primary motion, where you choose to play and not play. Clarity here is what makes the tactics that follow coherent.

beats.name: Product
beats.description: Highlight the unique value the product brings to the strategy. Lead with the customer outcome; tie it directly back to the customer beat. Avoid feature soup.

beats.name: Price
beats.description: Justify pricing and packaging. Show the logic — cost-plus, value-based, competitor-anchored — and the levers you'll use over the period. Price decisions are strategy decisions.

beats.name: Place
beats.description: Describe distribution channels and the role each plays. Direct, partner, marketplace, retail. Channel mix is often where strategies quietly succeed or fail.

beats.name: Promotion
beats.description: Reveal the campaign and content tactics that bring the strategy to market. Pair each tactic with the audience and metric it serves. Avoid listing channels for their own sake.

beats.name: Summary
beats.description: Recap the strategy in a single page: customer, position, motion, expected outcome. End with the decision or commitment you need from the audience.

narratives/performance-improvement-plan..name: Performance Improvement Plan
narratives/performance-improvement-plan..summary: Structured PIP arc that helps a struggling employee see expectations clearly, understand the gap, and walk into a credible improvement path. Designed to be respectful, specific, and outcome-focused — not punitive.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Begin respectfully and set a constructive tone. Be clear about what this conversation is and isn't. The opening shouldn't catastrophize or sugarcoat — clarity is kinder than either.

beats.name: Set Expectations
beats.description: Detail the level of performance expected in the role. Specific behaviors, deliverables, and standards. Expectations the employee can't quote back are expectations they can't meet.

beats.name: Identify Problems
beats.description: Name the gap between expected and observed performance. Use specific examples and dates rather than impressions. Avoid characterizing the person; focus on the work product and the impact.

beats.name: Possible Solutions
beats.description: Suggest improvement strategies tailored to the gaps named above. Behavior changes, structural changes, support structures. Frame them as paths the employee can choose, not orders to follow.

beats.name: Offer Resources
beats.description: Make explicit what tools, coaching, training, or peer support is available. Resources demonstrate that the organization is investing in the outcome, not setting the employee up to fail.

beats.name: Motivate Change
beats.description: Connect improvement to what the employee values: their growth, their team, their career. Inspire action without minimizing the seriousness of the situation.

beats.name: Follow Up
beats.description: Schedule the check-ins. Frequency, format, criteria for progress. Predictable follow-up turns a PIP from a threat into a plan.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Close with confidence in the path forward and a clear restatement of what success looks like. End the meeting having both raised the bar and reaffirmed the relationship.

narratives/performance-review.json.name: Performance Review
narratives/performance-review.json.summary: Analytical review of individual, team, or company performance grounded in metrics. Walks through results, key drivers, wins, challenges, and the adjustments that will shape the next period.

beats.name: Briefing
beats.description: Frame what this review covers: the period, the unit, the standard you're measuring against. One slide that lets the audience know exactly what they're being asked to evaluate.

beats.name: Results
beats.description: Lead with the headline result. On track, ahead, or behind, and by how much. Resist softening — clear numbers up front earn credibility for the analysis that follows.

beats.name: Key Metrics
beats.description: Walk through the pivotal indicators. One chart per metric, clear comparison period, target or benchmark visible on the same frame. Help the audience see the data the way you do.

beats.name: Team Performance
beats.description: Examine collective achievements and how the team contributed. Avoid generic praise; cite specific moves and the people behind them where the audience would expect it.

beats.name: Highlight
beats.description: Spotlight one standout contribution that defined the period. A landmark deal, a launch, a fix, a hire. One vivid example sticks longer than a list of accomplishments.

beats.name: Analysis
beats.description: Dig under the metrics. What drove the numbers, what held them back, what's signal versus noise. Analysis is where the audience learns whether you actually understand the system you're reporting on.

beats.name: Success
beats.description: Reinforce the past triumphs that show the system works. Briefly — the audience came for what's next, not a victory lap. Wins earn permission for the harder slides ahead.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Name the obstacles encountered honestly. What didn't move, what regressed, what the team is still wrestling with. Understated challenges read as missed signal, not modesty.

beats.name: Adjustments
beats.description: Identify the changes you're making in response. New tactics, reallocations, sunsets. Each adjustment should map to a challenge above — adjustments without diagnosis feel arbitrary.

beats.name: Strategy Evolution
beats.description: Show how the strategy itself evolves heading into the next period. Refinements, sharpened bets, dropped initiatives. The audience should see continuity as well as change.

beats.name: Discussion
beats.description: Open the floor with two or three specific prompts. End the review actively — questions you want answered, decisions you want made — so the meeting yields more than the deck.

narratives/persuade.json.name: Persuade
narratives/persuade.json.summary: Argument-driven keynote arc inspired by Ken Robinson: grip the audience, challenge the status quo, define the problem, anchor it in story and statistic, deliver a major revelation, propose change, and end on a question that stays with them.

beats.name: Gripping Introduction
beats.description: Open with a moment, image, or claim the audience can't easily look away from. The first sixty seconds buy you the next twenty minutes — spend them on something specific and emotionally charged, not on housekeeping.
beats.instructions: Draw in the audience with a compelling opener

beats.name: Challenge the Status Quo
beats.description: Call out the system, norm, or assumption that needs examination. Be precise about what you're disagreeing with so the rest of the talk can be specific in response. Avoid strawmen — name the strongest version of the view you're contesting.

beats.name: Present the Problem
beats.description: Define the issue the audience needs to care about. Concrete, scoped, attributable. The clearer the problem, the more credible the eventual solution.

beats.name: Personal Story
beats.description: Anchor the issue in a specific person, place, or moment. Story is what gets the argument past the audience's defenses. Pick a story that personalizes the data without overstating it.
beats.instructions: Share significant stories to illuminate the issue

beats.name: Statistic Shock
beats.description: Drop in a single statistic that recasts the scale of the problem. One number, presented well, lands harder than a dashboard. Cite the source so the audience can repeat it with confidence.
beats.instructions: Use impactful stats to highlight the gravity of the issue

beats.name: Historical Context
beats.description: Show how the issue evolved. Why it has the shape it does today, what was tried, what was missed. Historical context turns 'this is broken' into 'this stayed broken for these reasons.'
beats.instructions: Show the evolution or history of the issue

beats.name: Weave a Narrative
beats.description: Connect the threads — story, statistic, history — into a single argument. The audience should feel the case clicking together. This is the slide where rhetoric becomes architecture.

beats.name: Major Revelation
beats.description: Deliver the surprising or significant turn. The fact, finding, or reframing the rest of the talk has been earning. The revelation should redirect, not merely confirm.
beats.instructions: Deliver a surprising or significant discovery

beats.name: Propose Solution
beats.description: Advocate for the change you want. Concrete enough to be acted on, broad enough to inspire. Pair the solution with the smallest credible first step.
beats.instructions: Advocate for change or propose an actionable solution

beats.name: Final Question
beats.description: Close on a question rather than a summary. The right closing question follows the audience out of the room and into their conversations afterward.
beats.instructions: Finish with a thought-provoking question to stimulate audience thinking

narratives/persuasive-sales.json.name: Persuasive Sales
narratives/persuasive-sales.json.summary: Top-of-funnel sales arc that creates awareness and alignment with a prospective customer. Anchored in a market change, leading to your unique capabilities, supported by proof, ending with a clear call to action.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open with a brief framing of who you are and why this conversation is worth the prospect's next thirty minutes. Keep credentials short; the audience cares about their problem, not your résumé.

beats.name: Big Change
beats.description: Name the market shift the prospect's industry is living through. Make it concrete, recent, and undeniable. The change — not the product — is the reason they should care.

beats.name: Winners and Losers
beats.description: Show how the change is creating winners and losers in the prospect's space. Use named examples where you can. The goal is for the prospect to wonder which side they'll end up on.

beats.name: Benefits
beats.description: Paint the outcome a winner experiences: a vivid picture of the prospect's life on the other side of the change. Lead with what changes for them, not with what your product does.
beats.instructions: Describe benefits, paint a vivid picture

beats.name: Capabilities
beats.description: Reveal the unique capabilities that make those outcomes possible. Frame them as the 'magic gifts' the prospect needs to win the new game. Highlight what's structurally different from the alternatives.
beats.instructions: Present unique features as 'magic gifts' to the customer

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Share customer testimonials, case studies, and measurable outcomes from organizations like the prospect's. Pick evidence that maps to the benefits you promised, not generic logos.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Ask for the next step in the sales process. Be specific: a pilot, a workshop, a follow-on conversation with a named stakeholder. Make the smallest credible commitment that keeps momentum.

beats.name: Close
beats.description: Close with a final image and contact path. Leave the prospect with one line about why they're better off acting now than later, and clear instructions for how to engage.

narratives/pitch-deck.json.name: Startup Pitch Deck
narratives/pitch-deck.json.summary: The canonical investor-pitch arc, drawn from Sequoia and Y Combinator's templates. Optimized for 10–20 minute meetings with VCs and angels. Each beat answers the question an investor will ask next.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Open with the company name, logo, and a one-line tagline that doubles as a positioning statement. Set the visual tone for the deck. Keep it confident and uncluttered — this is the cover.

beats.name: Company Purpose
beats.description: State in a single sentence what the company does and why it exists. Should be immediately understandable without industry jargon. Often doubles as the answer to 'so what do you do?'

beats.name: Problem
beats.description: Describe the pain point you solve. Make it concrete with a specific user or customer scenario. The more visceral and recognizable the problem, the stronger the rest of the pitch lands.

beats.name: Why Now
beats.description: Explain the technological, regulatory, behavioral, or market shift that makes this opportunity possible today and impossible five years ago. Investors want to know why this is a window, not just an idea.

beats.name: Market Size
beats.description: Size the opportunity. Top-down (TAM/SAM/SOM) or bottom-up (units × price). Show how big the prize is if you win, and why this market is attractive to a venture-scale outcome.

beats.name: Competition
beats.description: Map the competitive landscape honestly. A 2x2 matrix or feature-comparison grid is fine; what matters is showing you understand the alternatives and where you uniquely fit. Naïve 'no competition' answers tank credibility.

beats.name: Solution
beats.description: Show how you solve the problem and why your approach is uniquely better. Lead with the outcome for the customer, then show the mechanism. This is where you connect problem to product.

beats.name: Product
beats.description: Give the product its own moment. Screenshots or a key visual that captures what users actually see and feel. Pick one strong frame over a montage of small ones.

beats.name: Demo
beats.description: Walk through the core user flow end-to-end. Show real software solving a real problem in a real workflow — not a marketing reel. If a live demo is too risky, use a tightly edited recording with narration.

beats.name: Traction
beats.description: Prove momentum with one credible headline metric. Revenue, users, growth rate, customer logos — whatever best shows the business is working. One strong chart beats five vanity numbers.

beats.name: Growth Drivers
beats.description: Show how the headline metric got there and where it's going. Cohorts, retention, expansion, channel mix — whatever explains the engine behind the number. Investors back the trajectory, not the snapshot.

beats.name: Business Model
beats.description: Explain how the company makes money. Pricing, unit economics, sales motion, payback period. Should answer: what does it cost to acquire a customer, and what do they pay you?

beats.name: Team
beats.description: Establish why this team uniquely wins this market. Founder backgrounds, relevant experience, prior outcomes, key advisors. Investors back people first; make the case.

beats.name: Financials
beats.description: Show the financial picture: historical revenue, burn, runway, and forward projection. Be conservative-but-credible — investors will discount aggressive numbers and reward defensible ones.

beats.name: The Ask
beats.description: State the round size, intended use of funds, and what milestones the capital takes you to. Be specific — investors should leave knowing exactly what you want and what they get.

beats.name: Closing
beats.description: Close on a strong final image: logo, contact info, and the one line you most want the investor to remember. Leave space for the conversation that follows.

narratives/problem-solution.json.name: Problem → Solution
narratives/problem-solution.json.summary: Classic business arc: name the pain, raise the stakes, present your fix, show how it works, prove it, ask. The default for sales decks, internal proposals, and most general business presentations.

beats.name: Hook
beats.description: Open with a striking question, statistic, customer quote, or moment that earns the audience's attention. The goal is to make them want to hear what comes next, not to convey information.

beats.name: The Problem
beats.description: Name the pain in concrete terms. Make it visceral and specific — describe who hurts, how, and what they're trying to do today that isn't working. Avoid abstractions; use real examples or scenarios the audience recognizes.

beats.name: Why It Matters
beats.description: Quantify the cost of inaction or the upside of action. Use numbers, trends, customer impact, competitive pressure — whatever makes the audience feel the size of the problem and care about solving it now rather than later.

beats.name: The Solution
beats.description: Reveal your approach and what it produces for the customer. Lead with the outcome, not the architecture. Keep it concrete: what does the audience get, and what changes for them?

beats.name: How It Works
beats.description: Show the moving parts that make the solution credible. Walk through the key mechanism, workflow, or technical insight that explains why this approach succeeds where others have failed. Enough detail to earn trust; not so much that you lose the room.

beats.name: Proof
beats.description: Demonstrate the solution works. Use customer logos, before/after metrics, demos, case studies, third-party validation — whatever de-risks the claim. One strong piece of proof beats three weak ones.

beats.name: The Ask
beats.description: State a clear, specific call to action. What do you want the audience to do, decide, or commit to next? Make the smallest credible ask that moves things forward, and make it unambiguous.

narratives/product-launch.json.name: Product Launch
narratives/product-launch.json.summary: Persuasive launch arc: open with brand, hook with a promise, set the conflict, raise the stakes, reveal the product, raise stakes again, sell, and call to action. Tuned for keynote-style launches and major announcement decks.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Open with the company brand and a confident visual. Set the tone — this is a moment, not a meeting. One slide that signals the audience is somewhere worth being.

beats.name: Promise
beats.description: Hook the audience with the promise of the talk. Tell them, in one sentence, what they're about to see and why it matters to them. Specific promises buy patient audiences.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Set the stage with the world the product enters. The customer reality, the market state, the unmet expectation. Context turns the launch from a product release into a moment in a larger story.

beats.name: Conflict
beats.description: Introduce the villain — the problem, friction, or status quo the product opposes. Make the conflict concrete enough that the audience can name a moment they've felt it themselves.

beats.name: Stakes
beats.description: Emphasize what's at risk if the conflict isn't resolved. Quantify, personalize, dramatize. Stakes are what convert a curious audience into an invested one.

beats.name: Reveal
beats.description: Showcase the product. One striking visual, one defining capability, one sentence that captures what's new. Earn the applause line; don't bury it under a bullet list.

beats.name: Raise the Stakes
beats.description: Highlight where the alternatives fall short and what they cost the customer. Re-energize the room midway by sharpening the contrast with the reveal.

beats.name: Reinforce the Need
beats.description: Reinforce why change is non-negotiable now. A second beat of stakes, framed differently — perhaps a customer voice or a future cost. Cement the reason to act.

beats.name: Sell
beats.description: Make the audience want the product. Lead with the outcome it produces in their lives. Pricing, packaging, availability go here, but only after the desire is built.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Close with the single action you want from the audience. Pre-order, sign up, attend, share. Make it simple, specific, and immediate.

narratives/project-proposal.json.name: Project Proposal
narratives/project-proposal.json.summary: Internal proposal arc for greenlighting a project: hook, problem, idea, benefits, justification, plan, timeline, risks, outlook, ask. Designed to take a sponsor from 'never heard of this' to 'approved' inside a single meeting.

beats.name: Elevator Pitch
beats.description: Open with the proposal in one slide: the project name, the audience, the goal, and the headline benefit. If a sponsor reads only this slide, they should still know what they're being asked to approve.

beats.name: Problem Statement
beats.description: Articulate the problem this project solves and why it deserves resources now. Tie it to a known business goal or pain. Vague problems produce vague approvals.

beats.name: Core Concept
beats.description: Describe the central idea of the project in plain language. The 'what' before the 'how.' A reader should be able to repeat the concept in one sentence after this slide.

beats.name: Benefits
beats.description: Quantify the impact: revenue, cost, risk, customer, capability. Use numbers where possible and clear comparisons where not. Each benefit should map to a metric the sponsor cares about.

beats.name: Justification
beats.description: Connect the project to broader strategy, OKRs, or constraints the audience already cares about. Show why this project is more important than the alternatives competing for the same resources.

beats.name: Approach
beats.description: Lay out how the project will be executed: the solution, the team shape, the budget envelope. Enough detail to feel credible, not so much that it pre-commits to choices that will mature in flight.

beats.name: Timeline
beats.description: Show the project phases on a timeline, with major milestones and decision points marked. Sponsors are buying a sequence of bets, not a single launch — make those bets visible.

beats.name: Risks
beats.description: Name the top risks honestly and pair each with a mitigation or open question. Listing risks without mitigations signals you haven't thought it through; hiding risks signals worse.

beats.name: Outlook
beats.description: Paint the picture of what the organization looks like a quarter or year after the project ships. Stretch beyond the immediate deliverable to the second-order benefits.

beats.name: Wrap Up
beats.description: Recap the proposal and state the specific decision you're asking for: approval, budget, headcount, sponsorship. Make it easy to say yes today.

narratives/pyramid-principle.json.name: Pyramid Principle
narratives/pyramid-principle.json.summary: Lead with your conclusion, then provide supporting logic. Respects audience time and attention.
narratives/pyramid-principle.json.description: Lead with the conclusion, then provide the supporting logic. State the main recommendation up front, follow with three or four arguments that support it, then back each argument with data and examples. The tone is deductive: conclusion first, reasoning second, so the audience never waits for the point. Best for executive presentations, recommendations, and time-constrained settings; typical decks run 3-8 slides (consulting recommendation, investment thesis, strategic options analysis).

beats.name: Answer First
beats.description: Lead with your main point or recommendation. Don't make executives wait for it.
beats.instructions: Lead with the conclusion or recommendation.

beats.name: Key Arguments
beats.description: Provide 3-4 supporting reasons that logically support your answer.
beats.instructions: Group the main reasons supporting the answer.

beats.name: Supporting Evidence
beats.description: Back each argument with data, examples, or proof points.
beats.instructions: Back each argument with verifiable proof.

narratives/qbr.json.name: Quarterly Business Review
narratives/qbr.json.summary: Standard QBR / business-review arc for internal leadership reviews. Recap commitments, show what the numbers say, separate wins from challenges, lay out the plan, surface risks, and request the asks the team needs to execute.

beats.name: Objectives
beats.description: Open with what this review is for and what decisions you want out of it. Frame the scope and the hour ahead, so the audience knows what they're being asked to weigh in on.

beats.name: Recap
beats.description: Briefly remind the audience what the team committed to last quarter and the high-level results against those commitments. Keep it terse — this grounds the review in prior context, but the meat is ahead.

beats.name: Performance Headline
beats.description: Show the top three to five KPIs with target vs actual and direction-of-travel. One slide that lets a busy executive grasp the quarter's outcome at a glance. Lead with the number, not the methodology.

beats.name: Performance Detail
beats.description: Drill into the supporting metrics by area or function. One chart per metric; clear y-axis, clear unit, clear comparison period. Call out anomalies before someone else does.

beats.name: Wins
beats.description: Highlight the quarter's biggest wins and who drove them. Be specific — name the deal, the launch, the customer, the team. Recognition belongs in the deck, not just in the meeting.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Name the misses and headwinds honestly. What didn't work, what's still hard, what got harder. Pretending things are fine costs more credibility than acknowledging they aren't.

beats.name: Insights
beats.description: Translate the numbers into 'so what.' What did the data tell you about customers, the market, your operations, your bets? Insights should be opinions backed by evidence, not restatements of the metrics.

beats.name: Next-Quarter Priorities
beats.description: Lay out the next quarter's top priorities. Each should trace clearly back to an insight or commitment. Three to five priorities, max — laundry lists are a tell that the team hasn't decided what matters most.

beats.name: Sequencing
beats.description: Show the order in which priorities ship and how they fit together. Dependencies, milestones, target dates. The audience should leave able to predict what comes when, not just what.

beats.name: Risks
beats.description: Name the risks to the plan honestly. Dependencies, assumptions, capacity gaps, market factors. For each risk, state the mitigation or the open question the audience can help resolve.

beats.name: Asks
beats.description: Specific, named requests of the audience. Decisions needed, resources required, escalations to unblock. End with clarity on what happens next and who owns it.

narratives/rags-to-riches.json.name: Rags to Riches
narratives/rags-to-riches.json.summary: Underdog journey from initial failure to eventual success. Pulls on resilience, grit, and perseverance — useful for founder stories, brand stories, and any deck where the audience needs to feel the cost behind the win.

beats.name: Origin
beats.description: Start at the bottom. Describe the humble beginning, the constraint, the moment before anything had been built. Concrete details — a place, a year, a feeling — earn the audience's investment in what follows.

beats.name: Inspiration
beats.description: Show the moment the protagonist found their calling. A conversation, a customer, a problem they couldn't unsee. The inspiration is the engine that pushes the rest of the story uphill.

beats.name: Opportunity
beats.description: Reveal the chance the protagonist took. Why this and not something safer? Make the choice visible — opportunities only count when there was something else they passed up to grab them.

beats.name: Adversity
beats.description: Walk through the hardest stretch. Concrete failures, near-misses, moments of doubt. Resist the temptation to skip past the pain — the audience trusts the win more when the loss was real.

beats.name: Overcoming
beats.description: Show how the obstacles got beaten. What changed, what was learned, what hard call was made. The transition from 'rags' to 'riches' should feel earned, not granted.

beats.name: Impactful Change
beats.description: Describe the moment the world tipped. The customer who said yes, the product that broke through, the metric that turned. One concrete transformation lands harder than a montage.

beats.name: Lasting Legacy
beats.description: Close on what the journey means for those who come next. The lesson, the people changed, the work that endures. Leave the audience with a takeaway that outlives the story.

narratives/reveal.json.name: Reveal
narratives/reveal.json.summary: Insight-driven keynote arc inspired by Amy Cuddy's 2012 talk on body language: connect through personal story, ground in research, illustrate with anecdote, summarize, break stereotypes, advise, demonstrate authenticity, close with impact. For talks that aim to change how the audience sees something they thought they understood.

beats.name: Personal Story
beats.description: Open with a personal experience that establishes why the topic matters to you. Specificity earns intimacy; intimacy earns the audience's permission to be moved.
beats.instructions: Share personal experiences to connect with the audience

beats.name: Research Exposition
beats.description: Lay out the scientific or empirical data that backs the premise. Be rigorous but not academic — the audience needs to understand the evidence well enough to defend it later.
beats.instructions: Unravel scientific data backing the premise

beats.name: Real-Life Anecdote
beats.description: Illustrate the research with a story from the field. Make the abstract finding feel like something that happens to people the audience could imagine being.
beats.instructions: Illustrate with stories to make the point relatable

beats.name: Critical Insights
beats.description: Summarize the two or three findings the audience must walk away with. Distill them into language a non-specialist could repeat without distortion.

beats.name: Break Stereotypes
beats.description: Question redundant norms or beliefs the research undermines. Be specific about what's being challenged so the audience knows what to update.
beats.instructions: Question redundant norms and belief systems

beats.name: Empowering Advice
beats.description: Translate the insights into a small, actionable practice. The advice should be doable today, not only next quarter — the goal is movement, not aspiration.

beats.name: Authenticity
beats.description: Speak honestly about your own struggle with the topic. Vulnerability, used with restraint, is what turns research into a felt truth.
beats.instructions: Honest and real communication to demonstrate authenticity

beats.name: Close With Impact
beats.description: End on a motivational high — the line, image, or invitation you want to follow the audience out of the room. Close the talk where it began, transformed.

narratives/scqa.json.name: SCQA (Situation–Complication–Question–Answer)
narratives/scqa.json.summary: Barbara Minto's pyramid-principle arc: surface the recommendation up front, then layer key arguments and supporting evidence beneath it. The default for executive memos, strategic recommendations, and consulting decks where the audience needs the answer fast.

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Establish the shared context: what is true today that the audience already agrees on. State only facts the audience accepts without argument. The goal is alignment, not persuasion — you are setting the stage.

beats.name: Complication
beats.description: Introduce the disturbance to the situation: what changed, what is at risk, what is no longer working. This is the tension that makes the audience lean in. Be specific and quantify the change where possible.

beats.name: Key Question
beats.description: Surface the question the complication forces the audience to answer. Frame it explicitly — 'Should we…?', 'How do we…?', 'What changes if…?'. The question should feel inevitable given the complication.

beats.name: Answer
beats.description: Deliver the recommendation in a single sentence, up front. No arguments yet, no caveats — just the conclusion the rest of the deck will defend. This is the apex of the Minto pyramid; everything that follows supports it.

beats.name: Key Arguments
beats.description: Lay out the two or three top-level reasons the answer is correct. One slide per argument, or one summary slide naming all of them. Each argument should stand alone as a compelling reason; together they should be exhaustive of the case.

beats.name: Supporting Evidence
beats.description: Present the data, examples, and case studies that ground each argument. Pyramid-principle style: every claim above is backed by something verifiable here. Cite sources; show the numbers; let the evidence carry the weight.

narratives/situation-complication-resolu.name: Situation-Complication-Resolution
narratives/situation-complication-resolu.summary: McKinsey-style structure that builds tension before delivering insights.
narratives/situation-complication-resolu.description: A McKinsey-style structure that builds tension before delivering the insight. Establish the context everyone already agrees on, introduce what has changed or what challenge has emerged, name the key question that change raises, then deliver the recommendation that resolves it. The tone is logical: a tight causal chain from context to recommendation. Best for strategy presentations, consulting decks, and analytical reports; typical decks run 4-10 slides (management consulting report, strategic recommendation, board update).

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Set the scene with relevant background and context everyone agrees on.
beats.instructions: State the shared context the audience already accepts.

beats.name: Complication
beats.description: Introduce what has changed or what challenge has emerged.
beats.instructions: Introduce the change, risk, or tension.

beats.name: Question
beats.description: Articulate the key question that the complication raises.
beats.instructions: Frame the decision question raised by the complication.

beats.name: Answer
beats.description: Deliver your recommendation or insight that resolves the question.
beats.instructions: Deliver the recommendation that resolves the question.

narratives/sparkline.json.name: Sparkline
narratives/sparkline.json.summary: A tight comparison arc showing the transformation from an inferior state to a superior one, anchored by contrast.
narratives/sparkline.json.description: A tight comparison arc that shows the move from an inferior state to a superior one, anchored by contrast. Make the painful before state vivid, reveal the product, decision, or event that changes the trajectory, present the new reality in concrete terms, then prove it with data or testimonial. The tone is contrastive: it makes the gap between old and new viscerally clear. Best for product demos, case study summaries, ROI presentations, and before-and-after technology comparisons; typical decks run 4-6 slides.

beats.name: Before State
beats.description: Make the current pain or limitation vivid with numbers, stories, or visuals that make the problem real.
beats.instructions: Make the current pain or limitation vivid.

beats.name: Contrast Moment
beats.description: Introduce the change agent, product, or decision that shifts the trajectory.
beats.instructions: Introduce the decision, product, or event that changes the trajectory.

beats.name: After State
beats.description: Show the improved reality. Make it concrete and specific instead of relying on vague benefit language.
beats.instructions: Show the new reality created by the change.

beats.name: Proof
beats.description: Validate the after state with metrics, testimonials, or third-party evidence.

narratives/star-method.json.name: STAR Method
narratives/star-method.json.summary: Results-focused framework that demonstrates impact through concrete examples.
narratives/star-method.json.description: A results-focused framework that demonstrates impact through a concrete example: the Situation, the Task you were responsible for, the Actions you took, and the measurable Result. The tone is evidential: every claim is grounded in a specific, verifiable outcome. Best for project reviews, portfolio presentations, and achievement showcases; typical decks run 4-8 slides (case study, customer success story, project retrospective).

beats.name: Situation
beats.description: Describe the context and background of the scenario.
beats.instructions: Describe the relevant context and constraints.

beats.name: Task
beats.description: Explain your specific role and responsibilities in this situation.
beats.instructions: Explain the responsibility or target outcome.

beats.name: Action
beats.description: Detail the specific steps you took to address the challenge.
beats.instructions: Detail the actions taken and choices made.

beats.name: Result
beats.description: Share the measurable outcomes and impact of your actions.

narratives/status-update.json.name: Status Update
narratives/status-update.json.summary: Concise progress-report arc for keeping a stakeholder informed: headline, brief, progress, results, plan, feedback. Optimized for short, repeated updates rather than one-time deep dives.

beats.name: Headline
beats.description: Open with the single most important sentence the audience needs to know — on track, off track, or shifted. The headline replaces 'how's it going' with a clear answer.

beats.name: Brief
beats.description: State the objective for the period and what was promised. One slide, three lines. Frames the rest of the update so progress is read against a clear bar.

beats.name: Progress
beats.description: Walk through the actions taken since the last update. Specific, attributable, dated. Avoid effort theater — list outcomes and material moves, not activity for its own sake.

beats.name: Results
beats.description: Show the outcomes those actions produced. Metrics, customer signals, decisions made. Keep the comparison crisp — versus plan, versus last period, versus benchmark.

beats.name: Action Plan
beats.description: Outline the next steps and who owns them. Be specific about the next decision point and what would have to happen to slip the schedule.

beats.name: Feedback
beats.description: Invite the audience to weigh in: where you'd like input, where you need a decision, where help would unblock you. End the update with an open hand, not a closed file.

narratives/strategic-advisory.json.name: Strategic Advisory
narratives/strategic-advisory.json.summary: Consulting-style advisory deck applying Minto's pyramid: title, situation/complication/question, the answer in one sentence, and three argued points with a process. Use when the audience expects a recommendation and the case for it, in that order.

beats.name: Title
beats.description: Open with a one-line summary statement that captures the recommendation, not the topic. The title slide is the headline of the entire engagement — make it specific enough that someone reading only this slide already understands the position.

beats.name: Situation, Complication, Question
beats.description: Frame the engagement on a single slide: the relevant status quo, what needs to change, and the question that needs to be resolved. This is the SCQ shorthand — context, tension, prompt. Don't yet answer.

beats.name: Answer
beats.description: Deliver the recommendation in a single sentence. No arguments yet, no caveats. The answer is the apex of the pyramid; the rest of the deck supports it.
beats.instructions: A solution in one sentence, no arguments yet

beats.name: Arguments
beats.description: Preview the three top-level arguments that defend the answer. One slide naming all three so the audience knows where the deck is going. Each argument should be a complete claim, not a topic.

beats.name: Argument 1
beats.description: Develop the first argument with supporting data, examples, and reasoning. Lead with the claim, then the evidence — Minto-style. The slide should stand alone if pulled out.

beats.name: Argument 2
beats.description: Develop the second argument the same way. Vary the type of evidence — quantitative, qualitative, comparative — so the audience hears the case from multiple angles.

beats.name: Argument 3
beats.description: Develop the third argument and walk through the supporting process or methodology. This is often where the 'how' lives — the implementation insight that makes the recommendation feel actionable.
beats.instructions: Third key point with a process

beats.name: Summary
beats.description: Recap the answer and arguments in a single slide and point to additional resources. Close with the explicit next step you want the audience to take.
beats.instructions: Recap the answer, provide additional resources

narratives/strategic-narrative.json.name: Strategic Narrative
narratives/strategic-narrative.json.summary: The change-driven founder/sales arc: a tectonic shift creates winners and losers, the audience must respond, and your product is the only credible way to land in the winners' camp. Used for top-of-funnel sales pitches, board re-positioning, and high-stakes founder talks.

beats.name: The Shift
beats.description: Open by naming a large, undeniable change in the world that the audience already half-believes. Technology, regulation, customer behavior, economics — pick the shift that recasts the audience's reality. The shift, not your product, is the protagonist of the first half of the deck.

beats.name: Winners and Losers
beats.description: Make the consequences of the shift concrete. Who wins, who loses, by how much, on what timeframe. Use specific examples — companies, products, segments — that have already moved or are about to. The audience should feel that standing still is the riskiest choice.

beats.name: Promised Land
beats.description: Paint a vivid picture of the future state your audience could occupy if they navigate the shift well. Describe outcomes, not features. The promised land must feel desirable, achievable, and meaningfully different from where they are today.

beats.name: Old Game
beats.description: Show why the existing playbook can't get the audience to the promised land. Name the legacy approach honestly and credit what it once did, then explain why the shift has rendered it insufficient. Avoid strawmen — the more fairly you state the old game, the more credible your new game becomes.

beats.name: New Game
beats.description: Introduce your category-defining approach as the way to play the new game. Show the principles or capabilities that make it possible only now. Emphasize what's structurally different from the old game, not what's marginally better.

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Prove the new game works. Customer outcomes, named logos, before/after data, third-party validation. Choose evidence that maps directly to the shift you opened with — proof that other audiences in the same boat made it to the promised land.

beats.name: Call to Action
beats.description: Close with the single decision you want the audience to make. Frame it as the obvious next move given the shift, the stakes, and the new game. Make it small enough to say yes to today and large enough to start a real engagement.

narratives/survey-analysis.json.name: Survey Analysis
narratives/survey-analysis.json.summary: Structured walk-through of survey results: topic, executive summary, methodology, findings, analysis, implications, recommendations. Built so a reader who only sees the second slide already knows the headline insight.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open by naming the question the survey was meant to answer. Why this, why now, who commissioned it. Anchor the audience in the decision the survey is designed to inform.

beats.name: Executive Summary
beats.description: State the top three findings in plain language on a single slide. A reader who only sees this slide should still be able to make the right call. Avoid hedging — synthesis is the point.

beats.name: Context
beats.description: Detail the situation behind the survey: prior knowledge, related research, the gap this work fills. Just enough to position the findings as new information rather than restated common sense.

beats.name: Data & Methodology
beats.description: Describe how the data was collected and from whom. Sample size, recruitment, instrument, timing. Be honest about limitations; methodological transparency is what gives the findings their weight.

beats.name: Data Summary
beats.description: Give the audience an overview of the dataset before drilling in. Demographics, response rates, distribution of key variables. Help them calibrate what 'most' and 'few' mean in this study.

beats.name: Findings
beats.description: Present the key insights one at a time. Lead each finding with the claim, then the chart. Avoid burying the point under the visualization — captions should restate the insight in words.

beats.name: Data Analysis
beats.description: Break down the data behind each finding: cross-tabs, segment splits, statistical confidence. This is the slide skeptics will scrutinize — make it scrutinizable.

beats.name: Implications
beats.description: Translate findings into 'so what.' What changes for product, marketing, ops, the customer? Implications without consequences are interesting trivia, not research.

beats.name: Recommendations
beats.description: Provide the actions that follow from the implications. Prioritize, attach owners, mark which require decisions. This is where research becomes useful.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Recap the headline finding and the most important recommendation. End with the next step — a follow-on study, a workshop, a decision — so the work doesn't sit on a shelf.

narratives/survival-story.json.name: Survival Story
narratives/survival-story.json.summary: Narrative arc of overcoming adversity through determination: catastrophe, backstory, plan, danger, effort, struggle, pivot, breakthrough, legacy, takeaway. For brand stories, founder histories, and leadership talks where the lesson lives in the comeback.

beats.name: Catastrophe
beats.description: Open in the middle of the disaster. Specific moment, specific stakes, specific damage. Drop the audience into the worst point of the story before walking them back.

beats.name: Backstory
beats.description: Detail the events that led up to the catastrophe. Just enough for the audience to understand how the disaster could have happened. Avoid moralizing — the story does the work.

beats.name: Blueprint
beats.description: Illustrate the recovery plan. Specific moves, specific bets, specific people. The audience should see the strategy as more than 'try hard.'

beats.name: Danger
beats.description: Highlight the emerging threats to the recovery plan. New risks, returning ones. Tension here makes the eventual triumph credible.

beats.name: Endeavor
beats.description: Show the determined effort underway. The hours, the trade-offs, the discipline. The audience must feel the work, not just hear about it.

beats.name: Struggles
beats.description: Showcase challenging moments along the way: the setbacks, the false starts, the hard calls. Honest setbacks make eventual success feel earned.

beats.name: Pivot
beats.description: Highlight the strategic shift that changed the trajectory. What got reconsidered, what got dropped, what got doubled down on. The pivot is the moment the protagonist became something new.

beats.name: Breakthrough
beats.description: Emphasize the moment adversity finally broke. Concrete result, concrete date. Let the slide land — the audience came for this turn.

beats.name: Legacy
beats.description: Discuss the enduring impact. What survival made possible afterward, who benefited, what was built on top. Survival stories are most powerful when they create more than they restore.

beats.name: Takeaway
beats.description: Share the lesson the audience can carry away. One transferable insight, framed for their own challenges — not a general moral.

narratives/transformation-arc.json.name: Transformation Arc (Before / After / Bridge)
narratives/transformation-arc.json.summary: Marketing-copy arc adapted for slides: paint the painful 'before,' contrast it with a vivid 'after,' then deliver the bridge that gets the audience from one to the other. Tight, persuasive, and ideal for short pitches, landing-page-style decks, and product-marketing teasers.

beats.name: Before
beats.description: Describe the audience's current world in the first person they recognize. Specific frustrations, specific costs, specific moments of friction. The clearer the 'before' lands, the more the rest of the deck has to push against.

beats.name: After
beats.description: Paint the world the audience could be in instead. Concrete outcomes, not feature lists — what a day looks like, what a quarter feels like, what becomes effortless that used to hurt. Make it desirable and credible at the same time.

beats.name: Bridge
beats.description: Show the path from before to after: the product, service, or change that closes the gap. Lead with the simplest user-visible thing they do; the architecture can wait. The bridge must feel proportionate to the transformation it promises.

beats.name: Evidence
beats.description: Prove the bridge has carried others across. One or two strong customer stories, before/after metrics, or named logos with concrete outcomes. Choose proof that maps directly to the 'after' you painted, not generic credibility markers.

beats.name: Ask
beats.description: Close with the single low-friction action that starts the audience across the bridge. Make it small enough to act on now and meaningful enough to count as commitment.

narratives/trend-analysis.json.name: Trend Analysis
narratives/trend-analysis.json.summary: Identify and discuss data-driven patterns to understand performance and forecast what's next. Useful for market reviews, strategic outlooks, and any deck where the audience must act on a direction-of-travel call.

beats.name: Introduction
beats.description: Open by establishing why this trend matters now. Tie it to a decision on the table or a forecast that's about to be made. Trends without consequences are filler.

beats.name: Historical Comparison
beats.description: Contrast current data with the relevant past. Pick the comparison window that makes the trend visible without cherry-picking. Be honest about base effects.

beats.name: Pattern Identification
beats.description: Name the recurring outcome you've spotted. Use one or two strong charts that show the pattern unambiguously. Avoid overclaiming significance from a small N.

beats.name: Future Prediction
beats.description: Project where the trend leads if it continues. Show the forecast and the confidence interval. State the assumptions that would have to break for the prediction to fail.

beats.name: Action Plan
beats.description: Translate the prediction into the strategy it implies. Specific actions, sequenced. Each action should map to a particular reading of the trend, not a generic best practice.

beats.name: Implementation
beats.description: Walk through how the actions get executed: owners, milestones, monitoring. The audience should leave understanding what to do tomorrow, not just what to think about.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Recap the trend, the forecast, and the recommended action. End with the leading indicator you'll watch to know if the call is right.

narratives/underdog-victory.json.name: Underdog Victory
narratives/underdog-victory.json.summary: Story arc of someone or something overlooked who triumphs in the end. Useful for founder narratives, brand stories, and team-building decks where the lesson is about resilience and unexpected wins.

beats.name: Origin
beats.description: Establish the opening scene: who the underdog is and the world that overlooked them. Specific details make the rest of the journey feel real.

beats.name: Struggles
beats.description: Highlight the early setbacks. What didn't work, who said no, where the path closed up. The audience needs to feel the doubt before they can feel the win.

beats.name: Determination
beats.description: Showcase the enduring passion that kept the underdog going. What they refused to give up on, and why. Determination, in this beat, is the only resource the underdog has.

beats.name: Crisis
beats.description: Identify the lowest point of the journey. The moment the dream nearly ended. Don't soften — the contrast with the triumph ahead depends on the depth of this slide.

beats.name: Resolve
beats.description: Articulate the choice the underdog made to keep going. The strong will, the small bet, the borrowed faith. Resolve is where the protagonist becomes someone the audience roots for.

beats.name: Breakthrough
beats.description: Show the reward of perseverance: the customer who said yes, the door that opened, the fortune that turned. The breakthrough should feel earned, not granted.

beats.name: Triumph
beats.description: Reveal the ultimate success. Concrete outcomes, named milestones. The triumph is the audience's emotional payoff — let it land.

beats.name: Legacy
beats.description: Share the lasting impact. What the underdog's victory makes possible for those who come after. The legacy beat is what turns a story into a lesson.

narratives/venture-pitch.json.name: Venture Pitch
narratives/venture-pitch.json.summary: Series A/B fundraising arc structured around the canonical investor questions.

narratives/vision-roadmap.json.name: Vision to Roadmap
narratives/vision-roadmap.json.summary: Connects a compelling long-term vision to near-term executable plans, bridging aspiration and action.
narratives/vision-roadmap.json.description: Connects a compelling long-term vision to near-term executable plans, bridging aspiration and action. Open with a specific three-to-five-year North Star, honestly diagnose the gap between today and that vision, organize the strategy into two to four named pillars, show the phased roadmap with milestones and dependencies, and end with concrete, assigned first steps for the next 30-90 days. The tone is inspirational and strategic: it creates shared direction and commitment to a plan. Best for strategic planning, annual kickoffs, product strategy, and OKR launches; typical decks run 8-20 slides.

beats.name: Vision
beats.description: State the 3-5 year North Star. It should be specific, memorable, and directional rather than generic.

beats.name: Current State Gap
beats.description: Honestly assess where you are today versus the vision. The gap justifies the plan.
beats.instructions: Define the gap between today and the vision.

beats.name: Strategic Pillars
beats.description: Organize the strategy into 2-4 named priority themes. Each pillar should be independently compelling.
beats.instructions: Name the strategic pillars that close the gap.

beats.name: Roadmap
beats.description: Show the phased execution plan with timeframes, milestones, and dependencies. Gantt or swim lane formats work well.

beats.name: First Steps
beats.description: Close with concrete, assigned actions for the next 30-90 days. Remove the gap between inspiration and execution.
beats.instructions: Identify the immediate moves that start execution.

narratives/weekly-progress.json.name: Weekly Progress
narratives/weekly-progress.json.summary: Tight rhythm-of-business arc for weekly progress reports: objectives, achievements, progress, challenges, opportunities, recognition, plan, discussion, conclusion. Designed for fifteen-to-thirty-minute team check-ins, not deep dives.

beats.name: Opening
beats.description: Open with the initiative name, the date, and the one-line headline for the week. Frame the meeting in fifteen seconds so the rest of the time is content.

beats.name: Objectives
beats.description: State what the team set out to do this week. Specific, measurable. The audience should be able to read this slide alone and know what 'on track' would mean.

beats.name: Achievements
beats.description: Celebrate the week's wins. Concrete, attributable, dated. Brevity here — the meeting is for what's next, not a victory lap.

beats.name: Overall Progress
beats.description: Evaluate performance against the objectives. Use a simple status indicator (green/yellow/red) plus the leading metric. Help the audience scan the state in seconds.

beats.name: Challenges
beats.description: Address what's hard right now: blockers, slipping items, surfaced risks. Tie each challenge to either an owner working it or a discussion you want this week.

beats.name: Opportunities for Improvement
beats.description: Surface where the team can level up. Process tweaks, tooling needs, ways of working. Improvement opportunities should feel like seeds, not corrections.

beats.name: Highlights & Recognition
beats.description: Recognize specific contributions by name. Recognition belongs in the deck, not just in the meeting — written acknowledgment travels further than verbal.

beats.name: Goals Next Week
beats.description: Plan the week ahead with three to five specific goals. Each should be small enough to finish, large enough to matter, and clearly owned.

beats.name: Discussion & Feedback
beats.description: Open the floor with two or three prompts — decisions you need, opinions you want, blockers you'd like cleared. End the recap actively.

beats.name: Conclusion
beats.description: Close with one line that motivates the team into the next week. Echo the headline so the meeting feels closed.

narratives/what-so-what-now-what.json.name: What-So What-Now What
narratives/what-so-what-now-what.json.summary: Concise framework that connects information to meaning to action. Perfect for executive audiences.
narratives/what-so-what-now-what.json.description: A concise framework that connects information to meaning to action. Present the facts or findings objectively, explain why they matter to this audience, then state the decisions or next steps they require. The tone is analytical: data-forward and respectful of executive time, with no scene-setting beyond what the facts need. Best for executive briefings, status updates, and research findings; typical decks run 3-6 slides (analytics report, team performance review, strategy update).

beats.name: What
beats.description: Present the facts, data, or findings objectively and clearly.
beats.instructions: Present the facts, data, or findings objectively and clearly.

beats.name: So What
beats.description: Explain the significance. Why should your audience care about this information?
beats.instructions: Explain the significance. Why should your audience care about this information?

beats.name: Now What
beats.description: Define the action required. What decisions or next steps follow from this?
beats.instructions: Define the action required. What decisions or next steps follow from this?

purposes/align.json.name: Align
purposes/align.json.summary: Create shared understanding and commitment across people who need to move together.
purposes/align.json.description: Use when stakeholders need a common view of goals, constraints, priorities, or responsibilities. Emphasize shared language, explicit tradeoffs, and next steps.
purposes/align.json.outcome: Stakeholders leave with the same priorities and operating assumptions.
successCriteria: Owners and next steps are clear

purposes/decide.json.name: Drive a Decision
purposes/decide.json.summary: Frame options, evidence, tradeoffs, and a recommendation so the audience can choose.
purposes/decide.json.description: Use when the deck exists to get a yes/no, select among options, approve a recommendation, or resolve ambiguity. Lead with the decision needed and make the ask explicit.
purposes/decide.json.outcome: The audience makes or authorizes a clear decision.

purposes/inform.json.name: Inform
purposes/inform.json.summary: Give the audience clear context, facts, or status without asking for a decision.
purposes/inform.json.description: Use when the deck needs to make the audience aware of current state, background, or findings. Prioritize clarity, completeness, and accurate framing over persuasion.
purposes/inform.json.outcome: The audience understands the situation and can repeat the important facts.
successCriteria: Audience can summarize the key facts
Follow-up questions are about implications, not basic context

purposes/persuade.json.name: Persuade
purposes/persuade.json.summary: Change belief or win support for a specific argument, idea, or recommendation.
purposes/persuade.json.description: Use when the audience may be skeptical or undecided. Build a crisp thesis, support it with evidence, address objections, and end with a clear action.
purposes/persuade.json.outcome: The audience accepts the argument or supports the recommendation.

purposes/pitch.json.name: Pitch
purposes/pitch.json.summary: Present an opportunity and ask for investment, approval, partnership, or sponsorship.
purposes/pitch.json.description: Use when the deck needs to create interest and move a high-stakes audience toward backing the opportunity. Lead with the opportunity, prove credibility, and make the ask concrete.
purposes/pitch.json.outcome: The audience agrees to invest, sponsor, approve, or continue the conversation.
successCriteria: Ask and next step are explicit

purposes/plan.json.name: Plan
purposes/plan.json.summary: Establish a roadmap, operating plan, or sequence of actions with owners and next steps.
purposes/plan.json.description: Use when the deck should turn strategy into coordinated action. Make sequencing, ownership, dependencies, risks, and checkpoints visible.
purposes/plan.json.outcome: The audience understands the plan and accepts the next actions.

purposes/report.json.name: Report
purposes/report.json.summary: Summarize performance, progress, or findings with enough context to interpret results.
purposes/report.json.description: Use for business reviews, project updates, research summaries, and recurring operating cadences. Prioritize the metric, the movement, the reason, and the implication.
purposes/report.json.outcome: The audience understands what happened, why it happened, and what it means.
successCriteria: Key metrics are easy to scan

purposes/sell.json.name: Sell
purposes/sell.json.summary: Move a buyer or evaluator toward purchase, adoption, renewal, or expansion.
purposes/sell.json.description: Use for customer-facing decks where the goal is commercial movement. Focus on pain, value, proof, differentiation, and the next buying step.
purposes/sell.json.outcome: The buyer advances to the next step in the commercial process.
successCriteria: Value is tied to customer outcomes

tones/authoritative.json.name: Authoritative
tones/authoritative.json.summary: Expert, declarative voice for category-defining and analyst-style decks.
tones/authoritative.json.description: Adopt the perspective of someone who's seen the full landscape and is willing to call it. Use plain declaratives — strong claims with the receipts to back them. Step back from internal-only context and frame in terms the wider industry would recognize.
voiceCues: Use declarative sentences; trust the reader to follow.
Frame in industry-wide terms, not company-internal language.
Cite outside sources — analysts, benchmarks, public peers.
Take a position; avoid 'on the other hand' symmetry without a verdict.
avoid: Hedging ('we believe', 'in our view') unless deliberately contrasting.
First-person plural overload — speak for the work, not the team.
Tentative phrasing that softens strong claims.
samplePhrases: Agent latency is the bottleneck of the next AI cycle.
Three categories will absorb 80% of enterprise budget; we're built for the second.
The benchmarks are public; the gap holds across every comparable workload.

tones/casual.json.name: Casual
tones/casual.json.summary: Warm, plain-spoken voice for internal updates and customer storytelling.
tones/casual.json.description: Friendly and direct. Use first- and second-person freely; favor short sentences and contractions. Numbers are still welcome — they just sit alongside human-scale framing rather than leading.
voiceCues: Use first and second person.
Use contractions ('we're', 'it's', 'don't').
Favor short sentences and active voice.
Frame metrics with a human-scale anchor when possible.
samplePhrases: We shipped the new dashboard last week, and customers are already moving over.
Here's where we ended up on hiring this quarter.
It's been a busy month — here's the recap.

tones/conversational.json.name: Conversational
tones/conversational.json.summary: Direct, dialog-style voice for podcasts, fireside chats, and small-group reviews.
tones/conversational.json.description: Sound like one half of a real conversation. Ask questions on the slide and answer them; keep paragraphs short; lean into examples over abstractions. Useful when the deck is meant to support a discussion rather than to lecture.
voiceCues: Ask a question on the slide, then answer it on the next.
Use second person — speak to the room, not at it.
Lean on stories and concrete examples over abstract framing.
Keep each idea to one short paragraph; let the dialog do the rest.
avoid: Stuffing slides — leave room for the discussion.
Inside-baseball references the room may not share.
samplePhrases: Why now? Two things changed in the last six months.
Here's the part that surprised us — and what we did about it.
If you take one thing from this section, take this.

tones/formal.json.name: Formal
tones/formal.json.summary: Polished, restrained voice for board, investor, and regulator audiences.
tones/formal.json.description: Authoritative without being cold. Use third-person constructions, full sentences, and concrete numbers. Avoid hedges and humor that depend on shared in-jokes; rely on clarity and precision to land.
voiceCues: Use third person and the corporate 'we' sparingly.
Lead with the recommendation, then evidence.
Quote concrete numbers; avoid round-tripping ranges.
Prefer full sentences to bullet fragments on key claims.
samplePhrases: Q4 revenue grew 18% year over year, led by enterprise expansion.
We recommend approving the Series B raise at $30M.
Net retention was 124%; gross retention was 96%.

tones/inspirational.json.name: Inspirational
tones/inspirational.json.summary: Aspirational, narrative-driven voice for keynotes, founders, and rallying cries.
tones/inspirational.json.description: Reach for shared belief and possibility, then ground it in something concrete. Use vivid imagery and rhythm; avoid collapsing into hype by always pairing aspiration with a real anchor.
voiceCues: Open with belief; close with action.
Use rhythm — paired phrases, repetition, deliberate beats.
Pair every aspirational claim with a concrete proof point.
Speak in present tense to make the future feel inevitable.
avoid: Stacked superlatives ('the very best, world-changing, revolutionary').
Dense data tables — push numbers into supporting slides.
samplePhrases: We're building the runtime that makes agents feel instant.
When latency disappears, what becomes possible?
The next decade of software belongs to teams who treat speed as a feature.

tones/persuasive.json.name: Persuasive
tones/persuasive.json.summary: Argument-led voice for sales, fundraising, and recommendation-driven decks.
tones/persuasive.json.description: Frame every section as an argument that builds toward an ask. Surface objections, answer them, and pair claims with the strongest available proof. Read more like a memo than a report.
voiceCues: Lead each section with the claim it's making.
Surface the strongest counter-argument and address it.
Pair every claim with proof — customer, benchmark, or analyst.
End on a clear ask with named owner and date.
avoid: Symmetrical 'on one hand / on the other' framing without a verdict.
Information for its own sake — every chart should advance the argument.
Passive endings without a clear ask.
samplePhrases: Adopting our runtime cuts inference latency 8× while preserving accuracy.
The most common objection — 'we'll be locked in' — is addressed by our open OPF spec.
We're asking for a $30M Series B to ship into the enterprise tier.

tones/technical.json.name: Technical
tones/technical.json.summary: Precise, evidence-led voice for engineering, research, and product-detail audiences.
tones/technical.json.description: Lead with the question or claim, then walk through the mechanism and the numbers. Use exact terminology; assume the audience can handle and prefers it. Diagrams, tables, and benchmarks are first-class.
voiceCues: State the claim, then the mechanism, then the evidence.
Use exact terminology — don't soften technical terms for general readability.
Quote benchmarks with conditions (cold/warm, p50/p95/p99, dataset, hardware).
Prefer diagrams and tables over prose paragraphs for structural information.
samplePhrases: p95 inference latency is 38ms on a single A100, down from 312ms on the prior runtime.
We replaced the streaming serializer with a batched protobuf path; throughput rose 4.2× under load.
The result holds for context windows up to 32k tokens; beyond that, see appendix B.
